To waylay someone means to intercept or stop them — usually by waiting for them — in order to do something to them or with them, often without their consent or at an inconvenient moment.

Think of it this way: you are on a path, moving toward your destination. Someone is already waiting ahead of you, hidden or not, and when you arrive, they step out and stop you. That act of deliberately waiting and then suddenly stopping you — that is waylaying.

1. The serious, physical sense: to ambush

This is the original and more intense use of the word. Here, to waylay means to lie in wait for someone and then suddenly attack, rob, or capture them. The person doing the waylaying has harmful or criminal intent.

The travellers were waylaid by a gang of robbers on the mountain road.

The soldiers feared being waylaid as they passed through the forest.

In this sense, the key ingredients are:

  • Premeditation — the attacker planned it and waited
  • Surprise — the victim doesn't know it's coming
  • Harmful intent — robbery, harm, or capture

2. The everyday, informal sense: to stop someone (unexpectedly) to talk to them

This is the more common modern use. Here, waylaying is not violent at all. It simply means catching someone — often when they're busy, on the move, or would rather not be stopped — in order to talk to them, ask them something, or get their attention.

She waylaid her boss in the corridor to ask about her promotion.

I was waylaid by my neighbour just as I was rushing out the door, and he talked for twenty minutes.

Reporters waylaid the politician as he left the building.

In this sense, the key ingredients are:

  • The person being waylaid is on their way somewhere — they are moving, busy, or in a hurry
  • The other person deliberately positions themselves to intercept — this isn't a coincidence; they waited or stepped in on purpose
  • It feels like an interruption — it delays or inconveniences the person

Whether used in the serious sense or the casual sense, waylay always implies an element of being caught off guard or stopped against one's flow. The person being waylaid didn't invite or expect the encounter.

This is what separates waylay from simply "stopping" or "meeting" someone. When you meet someone, there is often mutual agreement or coincidence. When you waylay them, one side deliberately set up the encounter — often without the other person's knowledge — and the effect is that the person is halted, delayed, or interrupted.

Because of this, even in casual conversation, the word carries a slight sense of inconvenience, ambush, or imposition — even when no harm is meant.

The word sits on a spectrum:

  • Lightest use: Someone stops you in the hallway to chat when you're busy — mildly inconvenient.
  • Middle use: A reporter or a persistent acquaintance catches you before you can escape — more forceful.
  • Strongest use: A robber or criminal lies in wait and attacks — dangerous and violent.

The context and surrounding words will tell you where on this spectrum the writer or speaker means.

The past tense and past participle of waylay is waylaid (not "waylayed" — that is incorrect).

✅ He was waylaid on his way home.
❌ He was waylayed on his way home.

The present participle is waylaying.

She kept waylaying her manager with questions.

In short: to waylay = to deliberately wait for and intercept someone, either to attack/rob them (serious sense) or to stop them for a conversation at an inconvenient moment (casual sense). The core idea is always: one person lies in wait, then stops the other — unexpectedly, and on the stopper's terms, not the stopped person's.
